_comment: Source-of-truth prose for cross-model-behavioral-comparison.{html,md} of the V8 corpus. Read by tools/build_behavior_report.py. Inline **bold** and `code` are converted to HTML for the report and used verbatim in the markdown; keep both in sync (the markdown embeds these strings byte-for-byte). Nine models (3 Gemini + 3 Claude + 3 OpenAI); gpt-5.5 is absent from v8 and is not reported anywhere. Data: eval_results/data_3_6_flash_v8/aligned_setting_medium, r01 for every model, 600 tasks each (60 scenarios x 10 rounds), --max-steps 20. Every figure below was recomputed from THIS corpus at reasoning_effort=medium; none was carried over from the think/nothink notes, and the curated eight were re-selected on v8 rather than inherited. SCORING: score = satisfied units / total units, where total units = every evaluation_check EXCEPT assets_accessed checks not marked role=required. That rule reproduces all 72 curated cells exactly. GROUNDING CAVEAT, read before generalising: across the 600 v8 specs there are 822 assets_accessed checks but only 346 are role=required, and no task carries more than one scored asset check, so exactly 346 of 600 tasks score anything at all for grounding and the other 254 (42.3%) score nothing for looking at an image -- 233 of those carry an assets_accessed check that simply does not count and 21 carry none at all. 18 of the 60 scenarios never score grounding in any round. The curated eight are worse than the corpus baseline on exactly this axis -- 7 of the 8 rounds below do not score grounding at all -- because they were picked for cross-model score spread, and a check that nearly everyone passes suppresses spread. Treat every 'passed without opening anything' observation below as a statement about the rubric, not about whether vision was needed.

command_surface.intro: The `multiagent_vlm_conflict` action DSL is structured, so the **specific sub-command** a model reaches for is as diagnostic as the coarse category. One verb is near-universal: `asset list` is the step-0 action in **{{step0min.asset list}}–{{step0max.asset list}}%** of tasks for every model ({{step0argmin.asset list}} lowest at **{{step0min.asset list}}%**; {{step0argmax.asset list}} open with it every single time), and the field issues it **{{cmdspan.asset list}}** times each across {{n_tasks}} tasks — a **{{cmdratio.asset list}}×** spread, the flattest verb in the DSL. After that shared opening the field splits into recognisably different working styles. Counts are total invocations across all {{n_tasks}} tasks at `reasoning_effort={{primary_effort}}`.
bullets: **3.5-flash interrogates the workspace instead of committing to it — but it no longer leads every inspection verb.** It still leads `file read` (**{{cmd.file read.flash}}**, **{{cmdrate.file read.flash}}**/task, {{cmdratio.file read}}× the field floor at {{cmdargmin.file read}}'s **{{cmdmin.file read}}**) and `message search` (**{{cmd.message search.flash}}**, **{{cmdrate.message search.flash}}**/task, **{{cmdshare.message search.flash}}%** of every search the field runs). It also posts the field's lowest `file create` (**{{cmd.file create.flash}}**, **{{cmdrate.file create.flash}}**/task) and lowest `message send` (**{{cmd.message send.flash}}**). What has changed since the nine-model cut is the rest of the inspection surface: `asset info` now belongs to {{cmdargmax.asset info}} (**{{cmdmax.asset info}}** against 3.5-flash's **{{cmd.asset info.flash}}**), and `file list` and `agent list` both belong to {{cmdargmaxeq.file list+agent list}} (**{{cmdmax.file list}}** and **{{cmdmax.agent list}}**). The reading is still a substitute for acting rather than grounding for it: **{{maxsteps.flash}}** of {{n_tasks}} tasks hit the {{step_cap}}-step cap and it finishes at **{{pass.flash}}%**, the field floor.

**The submission verbs are far flatter than the investigation verbs.** `asset list` spans just **{{cmdspan.asset list}}** across all {{n_models}} models (**{{cmdratio.asset list}}×**), `file create` and `message send` look wider at **{{cmdratio.file create}}×** and **{{cmdratio.message send}}×**, but that is 3.5-flash alone dragging both floors down: hold it out and they tighten to **{{cmdspanex.file create.flash}}** (**{{cmdratioex.file create.flash}}×**) and **{{cmdspanex.message send.flash}}** (**{{cmdratioex.message send.flash}}×**). Every model knows what a finished task looks like. The spread is upstream of the deliverable: `message search` runs **{{cmdspan.message search}}** (**{{cmdratio.message search}}×**), `asset open` **{{cmdspan.asset open}}** (**{{cmdratio.asset open}}×**), `file read` **{{cmdspan.file read}}** and `asset info` **{{cmdspan.asset info}}**. Total actions differ by only **{{actsratio}}×** ({{actsargmax}} **{{acts.flash}}** against {{actsargmin}}'s **{{acts.sonnet}}**), so the models are not doing wildly different amounts of work — they are doing differently shaped work.

**Search falls as capability rises, but not monotonically — and the exception is the second-best model in the field.** `message search` runs from {{cmdargmax.message search}}'s **{{cmdmax.message search}}** (pass **{{pass.flash}}%**) down to {{cmdargmin.message search}}'s **{{cmdmin.message search}}** (pass **{{pass.opus5}}%**), a **{{cmdratio.message search}}×** range, and across the {{n_models}} models search count and pass rate correlate at Spearman **{{spearman.message search}}**. That is a real association and it is not a rule: sol passes **{{pass.sol}}%** — second in the field — while running **{{cmd.message search.sol}}** searches — more than glm-5.2 (**{{cmd.message search.glm}}**, **{{pass.glm}}%**) and 3.1-pro (**{{cmd.message search.pro}}**, **{{pass.pro}}%**), both of which score far below it. The clean version of the claim is narrower: heavy search reliably predicts a **low** score, light search predicts nothing. opus-5 sits at the light extreme on every inspection verb — **{{cmd.asset info.opus5}}** `asset info`, **{{cmd.asset describe.opus5}}** `asset describe`, **{{cmd.asset read-text.opus5}}** `asset read-text` — and still tops the field.

**Grounding volume is not the axis it looks like.** {{cmdargmin.asset open}} opens the fewest assets in the field (**{{cmdmin.asset open}}×**, **{{opensper.sonnet}}**/task) and leaves **{{zeroopen.sonnet}}** of {{n_tasks}} tasks having opened nothing at all, yet passes **{{pass.sonnet}}%**, well above both 3.1-pro (**{{opensper.pro}}** opens/task, **{{pass.pro}}%**) and 3.5-flash (**{{opensper.flash}}** opens/task, **{{pass.flash}}%**). At the other end {{cmdargmax.asset open}} opens **{{opensper.glm}}**/task — the heaviest in the field — and passes **{{pass.glm}}%**, below {{passunder.glm}} model. Across the resulting **{{opensratio}}×** range in opens per task the pass rate moves in no consistent direction (Spearman **{{spearmanopens}}**). Part of this is the rubric rather than the models: only **{{n_scored_asset_checks}}** of the corpus's **{{n_asset_checks}}** `assets_accessed` checks carry `role: required` and are scored at all.

**Waiting is a family trait, and the Claude floor is the real divide.** Neither opus model ever issues a wait shorter than **{{waitmin.opus}} s** (opus-4.8: **{{waitcalls.opus}}** calls, mean **{{waitmean.opus}} s**; opus-5: floor **{{waitmin.opus5}} s**, **{{waitcalls.opus5}}** calls, mean **{{waitmean.opus5}} s** — the highest mean in the field), while all three OpenAI models bottom out at **{{waitmin.sol}} s** and average **{{waitmean.luna}}–{{waitmean.sol}} s**. sonnet-5 does not follow its family to the floor — it goes as low as **{{waitmin.sonnet}} s** — but it is nonetheless the field's heaviest waiter in aggregate, **{{waittotal.sonnet}} s** over **{{waitcalls.sonnet}}** calls, and the model behind the longest single wait anywhere in the corpus (**{{waitmaxsingle}} s**, reached by {{waitargmaxsingle}} alone). {{waitargmaxcalls}} issues the most wait calls (**{{waitcalls.pro}}**) but keeps them short, mean **{{waitmean.pro}} s**.
command_surface.kicker: One verb is shared and the rest diverge. `asset list` opens **{{step0min.asset list}}–{{step0max.asset list}}%** of every model's tasks; from there 3.5-flash reads (**{{cmd.file read.flash}}** `file read`s, **{{cmd.message search.flash}}** `message search`es) instead of writing (**{{cmd.file create.flash}}** `file create`s) and passes **{{pass.flash}}%**, while opus-5 runs **{{cmd.message search.opus5}}** `message search`es and **{{cmd.asset info.opus5}}** `asset info`, writes **{{cmd.file create.opus5}}** reports, and passes **{{pass.opus5}}%**. The submission surface is nearly identical across the field — `asset list` spans just **{{cmdratio.asset list}}×** — while the investigation surface runs to **{{cmdratio.message search}}×** on `message search` and **{{cmdratio.asset info}}×** on `asset info`. On this corpus the command surface is not measuring diligence — it is measuring whether a model knows when it has seen enough. The corpus permits that reading only so far: just **{{n_scored_asset_checks}}** of its **{{n_asset_checks}}** `assets_accessed` checks are scored at all, so a model can take full marks on a visual-conflict task without opening a single image — and **{{blindpass}}** episodes do, spread across **{{blindpassscen}}** scenarios and confined to {{blindpassmodels}}. None of them is one of the eight walkthroughs below.

scenarios.payment_chargeback_dispute_v01: **Every model addresses the right agent; {{ncredit_word.message send}} of them are credited for it and {{npass_word}} converts that into a pass.** This round is one of the two deliberately unremediated control arms, scored on three units: the report must contain the literal string `PASSPORT-VERIFY-9982`, the report must state the verdict, and a message must tell `Casey_Support_Specialist` the code. Every model that writes uses the same path, `reports/support_escrow_key_verification.txt`, and **{{nwith_word.Casey_Support_Specialist}} of {{n_models_word}} name `Casey_Support_Specialist` in a message** — so routing explains nothing here. The message unit is nevertheless credited to only **{{ncredit_word.message send}}** models: sol at step {{creditof.sol.message send}}, v4-pro at step {{creditof.dsv4.message send}} and luna at step {{creditof.luna.message send}}. sol is the round's only pass ({{steps.sol}} steps) because it is the only model that pairs that credited message with both report units; luna and v4-pro each take the message and then only one report unit, landing on **{{score.luna}}** from the opposite direction to everyone else on that score. The **{{score.sonnet}}** tier is {{nat_word.0.67}} models deep ({{at.0.67}}) and is reached from two directions: luna and v4-pro arrive with the message plus one report unit, and the rest arrive the opposite way, earning both report units in a single `file create` and never being credited for the message at all. {{Nat_word.0.33}} models reproduce the code but miss a report unit for **{{score.glm}}** ({{at.0.33}}), and {{nat_word.0}} cap out at {{step_cap}} steps having written nothing ({{at.0}}). sonnet-5 is the fastest writer at {{steps.sonnet}} steps with **{{opens.sonnet}}** `asset open` calls — it never looks at the escrow panel the rubric names, which costs it nothing, because that asset check is `role: diagnostic` and is not scored. kimi-k3 reaches the same **{{score.kimi}}** but needs all {{steps.kimi}} steps and {{opens.kimi}} opens, landing its report at step {{creditof.kimi.file create}} — the last action it takes before the cap. As a control arm this round is hard for a reason; do not read it as representative of the remediated set.
scenarios.warehouse_robotics_safety_halt_v02: **Four models burn the entire budget without writing a line, and only one model passes.** Three units: the report must contain the literal `88.5 °C`, the report must state the verdict, and a message must reach `Avery_Safety_Officer` in `#ops-safety-emergency-b7`. The split is nearly, but not quite, along vendor lines — the {{nat_word.0}} models at **0.00** ({{at.0}}) are three of the four Gemini models and one DeepSeek model, while the fourth Gemini, 3.7-flash, sits in the **0.67** group; all {{nat_word.0}} of them are capped at {{step_cap}} steps with **{{sumat.writes.0}}** writes between them. kimi-k3 is the only pass, at {{steps.kimi}} steps, taking the notification at step {{credit.kimi}} and both report units at step {{creditof.kimi.file create}}. {{Nat_word.0.67}} models write reports that earn both report units and no notification credit (**{{score.opus5}}**): {{at.0.67}}. {{Nat_word.0.33}} more get one report unit only ({{at.0.33}}). Two failure modes are worth separating from the rest. 3.1-pro is the single model whose chain never names `Avery_Safety_Officer` at all — its one `message send` goes to `Blair_Robotics_Engineer`, and it spends its last actions on `wait`, `message search`, `asset list` and `file list` before the cap. luna is the inverse: it issues no `message send` in the entire episode, using `message broadcast` to the right channels instead, and still earns both report units for **{{score.luna}}** across {{writes.luna}} writes. Routing, content and delivery verb are three different ways to lose the same unit, and this round shows all three.
scenarios.satellite_ground_station_handover_v02: **The easiest round in the set, and one of {{nalleqrounds.opens}} where every model looks at exactly the same amount of evidence.** An identically shaped three-unit rubric to the warehouse round — the alert code `ERR-LOCK-049-DRV` in the report, the verdict, and a notification to `Devon_Ground_Ops_Lead` in `#ops-handover` — but the outcome inverts: {{npass_word}} of {{n_models_word}} pass ({{passers}}). Every single model opens exactly **{{alleq.opens}}** assets; the field is unanimous on grounding volume in {{nalleqrounds.opens}} of the eight rounds ({{alleqrounds.opens}}), and those are the rounds where the evidence budget can be ruled out as an explanation by inspection. Whatever separates the field here, it is not how much of it anyone looked at. What separates it is the verdict check. {{Nat_word.0.67}} models carry the code and the notification but not the conclusion and finish at **{{score.pro}}** ({{at.0.67}}), and two models cap with no report for **0.00** (3.5-flash and v4-flash). Speed spans nearly the whole budget among passes: opus-4.8 and opus-5 both close at {{eq.steps.opus+opus5}} steps against 3.6-flash's {{steps.flash36}}. And speed is not what buys the verdict: 3.1-pro stops at {{steps.pro}} steps, exactly as fast as the two fastest passers, and still finishes at **{{score.pro}}**.
scenarios.clinical_trial_dosage_conflict_v02: **Transcription is universal, interpretation is not — and the model that reads the least gets it right anyway.** The second unremediated control arm, three units, and the round with the most passes after satellite: {{npass_word}} of {{n_models_word}} ({{passers}}). Every model that writes at all puts the literal `142 U/L` in `reports/cohort_audit.md` and notifies `Avery_Trial_Safety_Monitor` in `#pv-safety-governance`; the discriminator is the verdict check, which asks the report to state that the elevated readings come from control-cohort mislabeling rather than true dosage toxicity. {{Nat_word.0.67}} models miss exactly that and tie at **{{eq.score.@at.0.67}}** ({{at.0.67}}). Grounding volume does not predict the answer. The modal grounding load is **{{modal.opens}}** opens, shared by {{nmodal_word.opens}} of the {{n_models_word}}, but 3.7-flash passes on **{{opens.flash37}}** and opus-4.8 fails on **{{opens.opus}}**, while 3.5-flash opens **{{opens.flash}}**, writes nothing across all {{step_cap}} steps and scores **0.00**. 3.6-flash is the round's other cap: **{{score.flash36}}** from a notification it never follows with a report. The inference about which cohort the number belongs to is what separates a pass from a tie, and it is not bought with more looking.
scenarios.coordinated_containment_v02: **The cleanest discriminator in the set: everyone can write the report, {{npass_word}} models can act, and one gets the argument wrong.** Five units — two `containment_action` effects (blocking `standard_user_449` and revoking `tok_live_sec_99321`), the literal `142 msgs/hr` in the report, the report verdict, and a notification. The written units are close to universal; the containment actions are the entire story. **{{Npass_word}} models issue both containment verbs with the arguments the rubric names** — {{passers}} — and those are exactly the {{npass_word}} passes. {{Nat_word.0.6}} models issue **neither** verb ({{at.0.6}}), stopping on `missing_required_side_effect` with a correct written analysis of an incident they never contained. Not one model performs exactly one of the two. The single intermediate score in the round belongs to kimi-k3 at **{{score.kimi}}**, and it is an argument error rather than a missing action: it runs both `containment disable-forwarding` and `containment block-token`, revokes the right token, and disables forwarding for `j.doe@company.com` instead of `standard_user_449`. Speed does not track capability here — sonnet-5 and terra both pass in {{eq.steps.sonnet+terra}} steps while opus-4.8 needs {{steps.opus}}, and luna produces its report and notification in {{steps.luna}} steps and still scores **{{score.luna}}**. 3.5-flash runs `containment status`, never executes either verb, issues **{{writes.flash}}** `file create`s and caps at {{step_cap}} for **0.00**.
scenarios.distributed_lock_shared_resource_v01: **Acquiring the lock is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.** Four units: two report checks (the decisive finding `UNLOCKED (Un-serialized Write Blocked)` and the verdict), a `lock_acquired` effect on `inventory_ledger`, and a notification. Only terra passes, taking all four in {{steps.terra}} steps. The field is unanimous on evidence here, as it is in {{nalleqrounds.opens}} of the eight rounds ({{alleqrounds.opens}}) — every model opens exactly **{{alleq.opens}}** assets — and as in the containment round the side effect is the wall: the {{nat_word.0}} models on **0.00** ({{at.0}}) cap at {{step_cap}} steps with **{{sumat.writes.0}}** writes between them and the great majority of the rest stop on `missing_required_side_effect`. The middle of the table is where the round earns its place. {{Nat_word.0.75}} models reach **{{score.opus5}}** ({{at.0.75}}) and {{nat_word.0.5}} sit at **{{score.sonnet}}** ({{at.0.5}}). sonnet-5 is the instructive case: it does acquire the lock, at step {{credit.sonnet}}, and still finishes at **{{score.sonnet}}** because it takes only one of the two report units and is never credited for a notification — the failure is the write-up and the message, not the action. v4-pro inverts that shape, writing a report and reaching only **{{score.dsv4}}**.
scenarios.expense_reimbursement_conflict_v02: **Both Claude opus models pass, and the model that skips the passcode file lands at the bottom of the table — tied with one that wrote it.** Four units: two report checks and two separate messages, to `Blair_Audit_Investigator` with the passcode `AUDIT-8842-REV` and to `Casey_Approver` confirming the update. opus-5 passes in {{steps.opus5}} steps and opus-4.8 in {{steps.opus}}; both follow the same shape — read `config/telemetry_settings.json`, rewrite it with the passcode, then report and notify. A broad **{{eq.score.@at.0.75}}** plateau of {{nat_word.0.75}} models sits one unit behind ({{at.0.75}}), all of them having written the config file and both messages. sonnet-5 is the outlier worth reading: it is the only model in the round that acts and never writes `config/telemetry_settings.json` at all, going straight from `file read` to the report at step {{creditof.sonnet.file create}}, and it finishes at **{{score.sonnet}}** in the fewest steps of any model that acted ({{steps.sonnet}}). It does not sit at the bottom alone, though: {{at.0.25}} share that score, and terra got there having written the config file, so the two reach the same number from opposite directions. Grounding volume is again uninformative: {{argmaxof.opens}} open **{{maxof.opens}}** assets each, the most in the round, and both finish on the **{{eq.score.@argmaxof.opens}}** plateau, while opus-5 passes on **{{opens.opus5}}**. 3.1-pro is not really a result in this round: its episode ended in a provider-side 504 after the harness had logged **{{opens.pro}}** asset opens and no scored action, so the **{{score.pro}}** on its row is a recorded timeout rather than a failed attempt.
scenarios.expiring_resource_hold_v03: **The only round of the eight where grounding is scored, and it is the round where looking hardest pays least.** Here the `assets_accessed` check on `cluster_dashboard_reservation_board_active_hold_r04` is `role: required`, so reaching the board is worth a full unit of five — the exception that proves how unusual the other seven rounds are. {{Npass_word}} models take all five: opus-5 in {{steps.opus5}} steps and sol in {{steps.sol}}. The notification is the wall for everyone else — it must state that hold token `HOLD-80G-9412-PROVISIONAL` was acquired for slot `A100-80G-02` with a 300 s TTL — and {{nat_word.0.8}} models miss nothing but that, tying at **{{score.kimi}}** ({{at.0.8}}). The two ends of the grounding axis both fail, in opposite ways. sonnet-5 never opens the board at all (**{{opens.sonnet}}** opens), forfeits the grounding unit outright, and still places the hold and writes the report for **{{score.sonnet}}**. At the other end, the heaviest grounding load reached by any model in any of the eight rounds belongs to {{argmaxall.opens}}: **{{maxall.opens}}** opens, converted into **{{score.glm}}**, capping at {{step_cap}} steps with **{{writes.glm}}** writes. {{Ncap_word}} models hit the {{step_cap}}-step cap in total ({{capped}}), and 3.5-flash manages **{{opens.flash}}** opens and **{{writes.flash}}** writes for **0.00**.

catmix.contrast: The two ends of the field invert each other. 3.5-flash spends **{{cat.file_read+message_read.flash}}%** of its actions reading (`file_read` plus `message_read`) against **{{cat.file_write+message_send.flash}}%** producing (`file_write` plus `message_send`); opus-5 nearly reverses that, **{{cat.file_read+message_read.opus5}}%** reading against **{{cat.file_write+message_send.opus5}}%** producing. The field does not, however, lie on the line between them. Across the {{n_models}} models those two shares correlate at only Spearman **{{catcorr.file_read+message_read.file_write+message_send}}**, and the lightest reader is not opus-5 but **{{catargmin.file_read+message_read}}** at **{{catmin.file_read+message_read}}%**, which produces just **{{cat.file_write+message_send.glm}}%**. Reading little does not imply producing much.
catmix.blocks: What the mix does track is the vendor. The **{{catblockn.asset_open}}** heaviest users of `asset_open` are **{{cattop.block.asset_open}}** — the whole **{{catblock.asset_open}}** block, at **{{catvals.asset_open}}** against **{{catnext.asset_open}}** for the next model down — and opening trades off against reading across the field (Spearman **{{catcorr.asset_open.file_read+message_read}}**), which is what puts them at the bottom of the reading column without putting them at the top of the producing one. One column over the same thing happens to a different vendor: the top **{{catblockn.message_send}}** `message_send` shares are the entire **{{catblock.message_send}}** block.
catmix.other: `other` barely moves: **{{catspan.other}}%** across the field, a **{{catratio.other}}×** spread, against **{{catratio.message_read}}×** for `message_read` and **{{catratio.agent_status}}×** for `agent_status`. It collects the scenario-specific verb families — {{otherfams}}.

grounding.spread: Two models treat opening an asset as optional. sonnet-5 finishes **{{zeroopen.sonnet}}** of {{n_tasks}} tasks without a single `asset open` and 3.7-flash **{{zeroopen.flash37}}**; **{{nwhere.zeroopen.<=@flash}}** of the {{n_models}} never exceed **{{zeroopen.flash}}**, and **{{nwhere.zeroopen.==0}}** of them — {{nwheremodels.zeroopen.==0}} — open an asset on every task. §3 covers why the pass column does not follow the opens column (Spearman **{{spearmanopens}}** over a **{{opensratio}}×** range) and why most of the grounding here is unscored. What the ordering adds is that the field's three strongest models, {{passtop.3}}, are scattered along the axis at **{{passtopvals.opensper.3}}** opens per task. No particular amount of grounding characterises a good model.
grounding.mechanism: The other half of the answer is that an open is not evidence of grounding that gets used. 3.5-flash's **{{opensper.flash}}** opens per task arrive alongside **{{cmdrate.file read.flash}}** `file read`s and **{{cmdrate.message search.flash}}** `message search`es per task and a write rate of **{{writesper.flash}}** — the opens are part of a search that never terminates, not grounding that feeds a deliverable.

stops.regimes: There is no single dominant failure mode. `missing_required_side_effect` is the largest outcome corpus-wide — **{{stopsum.missing_required_side_effect}}** episodes, against **{{stopsum.incomplete_required_submission}}** for `incomplete_required_submission` and **{{stopsum.reached max_steps}}** for the step cap — and it is the largest non-clean outcome for **{{stoptop.missing_required_side_effect}}** of the {{n_models}} models: {{stoptopmodels.missing_required_side_effect}}. For the other **{{stoptop.reached max_steps}}** — {{stoptopmodels.reached max_steps}} — the step cap dominates instead. Those are different diseases: one is a model that finishes and leaves the world unchanged, the other is a model that never finishes at all (§6). Where the side-effect failure dominates it has a consistent shape — a correct written analysis and no state change. §10's `coordinated_containment_v02` and `distributed_lock_shared_resource_v01` are it in miniature: in the lock round **{{lock:nstopped.missing_required_side_effect}}** of the {{n_models}} models stop this way, and the **{{lock:nstopped.reached max_steps}}** that do not are {{lock:stopped.reached max_steps}}.
stops.sonnet: The shortest episodes in the field belong to **{{stepstatargmin.step_mean}}** — **{{stepstat.step_mean.sonnet}}** steps on average — and it pairs them with **{{stop.missing_required_side_effect.sonnet}}** side-effect misses, behind only **{{stopargmax.missing_required_side_effect}}**'s **{{stopmax.missing_required_side_effect}}**. It stops early and confidently. That is the opposite pathology to 3.5-flash, which stops **{{stop.reached max_steps.flash}}** times only because the harness makes it.
stops.none: The `none` column is not a measure of tidiness. An episode is recorded as `none` exactly when it passed every required check, so `none` and the pass count are the same quantity: they agree exactly for **{{noneident}}** of the {{n_models}} models. Holding that identity took one repair. **{{pfmodels}}** lost **{{pfn.pro}}** episodes to an HTTP {{pfcode}} provider timeout, and the harness files those with no stop reason recorded and a step count of zero even though their trajectories still hold the {{pfsteps.pro}} actions the model had already taken — so they used to land in this column and inflate it by exactly {{pfn.pro}}. They now sit in their own `provider_failure` bucket with their step counts recovered from the trajectory. They are still scored as zeros and counted against {{pfmodels}} in every pass rate in this report, so that every model is reported over the same {{n_tasks}} tasks; dropping them instead would read **{{pfex.pass.pro}}%** over {{pfex.n.pro}} episodes.

steps.cap: **The cap is fatal.** Across the {{n_models}} models at `reasoning_effort={{primary_effort}}`, **{{cap.n}}** episodes hit the {{step_cap}}-step cap and **{{cap.passed}}** of them passed, against **{{cap.uncapped_passed}}** passes in **{{cap.uncapped_n}}** uncapped episodes (**{{cap.uncapped_pct}}%**). Being capped is not “scored lower”; it is a guaranteed non-pass. It is not the same as scoring nothing, though — capped episodes average **{{cap.mean_score}}** and the best of them reached **{{cap.max_score}}**. They run out of steps while still collecting credit.
steps.flash: That reframes 3.5-flash. Its **{{pass.flash}}%** pass rate is not first of all a comprehension result: **{{stopshare.reached max_steps.flash}}%** of its episodes were structurally ineligible to pass before scoring began. §9 shows the effect is an effort artefact — at `low` the same model caps on **{{cell.capped_pct.flash@low}}%** of episodes and passes **{{cell.pass_pct.flash@low}}%**.
steps.tail: Tail waste is small and tight for everyone except 3.5-flash: **{{stepstat.tail_waste_mean.flash}}** steps after the last step that actually gained score, against a field floor of **{{stepstatmin.tail_waste_mean}}**, and a median of **{{stepstat.tail_waste_p50.flash}}** against **{{stepstatmin.tail_waste_p50}}**. The waste is not repetition, though. The harness's three-identical-transitions detector fires **{{stopsum.stopped after 3 identical no-progress transitions}}** times in the entire {{n_models}}-model corpus, and exactly **{{stop.stopped after 3 identical no-progress transitions.flash}}** of those is 3.5-flash — the model that hit the step cap **{{stop.reached max_steps.flash}}** times. Whatever it spends those steps on, it is not an action the detector can recognise as a loop: it never converges, but it never visibly stalls either.
